To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) keyphrases can indeed be extracted from errorful Speech Recognition transcriptions, and (b) the keyphrases extracted from the multiple hypotheses are not more accurate than those extracted from a single best hypothesis.

keyphrase extraction from spoken audio documents is feasible, that keyphrase words tend to have a lower W ER than non-keyphrase ones and that multiple hypotheses for an utterance do not improve keyphrase extraction precision.

keyphrase extraction from spoken documents is a robust task that is relatively unaffected by speech recognition errors and that it is not necessary to use multiple hypotheses in the keyphrase extraction process.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question: "What is the minimum speech recognition quality that is required to support keyphrase extraction?". We conclude that keyphrases extracted from transcripts with WERs as high as 40% are of sufficient quality to be used in an interactive browsing system.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
keyphrases are easier to extract than full text transcription from speech recognition transcripts.
we can reliably extract keyphrases from transcripts that are 2-3 times worse than the transcripts that are used to train Extractor.
keyphrases are robust to speech recognition errors, and that the keyphrase extraction system we use is robust to the presence of multiple hypotheses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
keyphrases extracted from transcripts of spoken documents can be used as a basis for browsing and summarising them.
keyphrase extraction can provide an easy-to-use, low-cost alternative to full transcription for many applications.
keyphrase extraction from spoken documents is feasible, but it needs to be done in a robust fashion, taking into account the errors in the transcript.
